Circular genome visualizations are essential for exploring structural variants and gene regulation.

We introduce AuraGenome, a large language model (LLM)-powered framework for rapid, reusable, and scalable generation of multilayered circular genome visualizations.

We created a visualization tool, called Circos, to facilitate the identification and analysis of similarities and differences arising from comparisons of genomes.
Circos is effective in displaying variation in genome structure and any other kind of positional relationships between genomic intervals.
Such data are routinely produced by sequence alignments, hybridization arrays, genome mapping, and genotyping studies.

Circos uses a circular ideogram layout to facilitate the display of relationships between pairs of positions by the use of ribbons, which encode the position, size, and orientation of related genomic elements.
Circos is capable of displaying data as scatter, line and histogram plots, heat maps, tiles, connectors and text.
Bitmap or vector images can be created from GFF-style data inputs and hierarchical configuration files, which can be easily generated by automated tools.
This makes Circos suitable for rapid deployment in data analysis and reporting pipelines.

Advances in speed, quality, and affordability of whole genome analysis, including genome sequencing, have transitioned the comparative genomics field from comparing reference sequence assemblies to comparing assemblies of individual genomes.
Inter-species analysis leverages information about one species to further the understanding of biological mechanisms in another.
Comparative methods are now used to discover differences between individuals.

The application of a germane data representation and its corresponding visualization to a domain-specific problem has historically improved the effectiveness of data presentation, analysis, and dissemination.
In some cases, the benefit of a new approach has altered how data are perceived and investigated.
Tree maps have been applied to show distribution of disk usage on a file system (Johnson and Shneiderman 1991) and hierarchical biological data (McConnell et al. 2002).
Directed graphs have been used to depict networks, pathways, and phylogenetic information (Ciccarelli et al. 2006; Darwin 1859; Letunic and Bork 2007).
Clustered heat maps have been used to visualize array and expression data (Eisen et al. 1998; Sneath 1957).
Effective visualizations exemplify virtues such as clarity, a high data-to-ink ratio (Tufte 1992), and favorable scaling characteristics.
These visualization approaches have been widely adopted because they addressed pressing visualization problems within domains where data sets were previously opaque to effective visual inspection.
A pressing visualization problem exists in the domain of comparative genomics, specifically in the comparative genomics of individuals.
A visual paradigm is needed to display relationships between genomes to leverage large amounts of sequence data and expand the power of personal genomics.
Previous efforts to visualize positional relationships used linearly arranged ideograms connected by lines to represent rearrangements.
One approach uses encoding in HSL (hue, saturation, lightness) color space to perform three-way comparisons.
The methods in these approaches are effective for illustrating local alignments between similar sequences.

The shortcoming of the linear layout becomes apparent in representations associating many ideograms with numerous relationships, where multitudes of lines transgress unrelated ideograms and make patterns difficult to discern.
Color maps are used to mitigate overburdened visualizations by mapping a position pair onto a position and a color.
Color maps reduce the texture and richness of the data despite addressing the problem of overburdened visualizations.
Circularly arranged ideograms are prevalent in visualizations of microbial genomes, which are circular.
At least one report combined paired-position data with a circular layout to show relationships between genomic positions, specifically pathways.
The report hinted at the benefit of adopting the circular layout for application to structural data.

Visualization plays a central role in the analysis of genomic data as an efficient approach for data exploration and knowledge communication.

The human genome is a hierarchical structure.
A genome consists of one or multiple chromosomes.
Chromosomes are subdivided into smaller regions called genes (feature sets or features).
At the lowest level of hierarchy, genomes are composed of building blocks called nucleotides (A, C, G, and T).
The hierarchical structure makes it possible to measure data at different granularities.
Data can be recorded at the individual nucleotide level, known as point granularity (e.g., single nucleotide polymorphisms, or SNP, that covers only one nucleotide).
Data can also be measured at a gene level, leading to a segment granularity dataset (e.g., genes whose protein-coding regions cover more than one nucleotide).
The density of information varies for genomes.
In some experiments, data is recorded for each nucleotide, leading to a contiguous data density (e.g., DNA conservation scores, which are generally available for each position in a genome).
In other cases, the data may be sparse (e.g., genes that only cover a relatively small proportion of the genome), leading to empty and missing values.
Genome datasets can include network-based data and spatially mapped data.
Network data in genomes generally represent connectivity between distant regions of a genome (e.g., physical interactions between different locations in the folded genome).
Network data may also represent connectivity between two different genomes (e.g., synteny).
The type of data recorded for genomes, also called expression levels, can be three main abstract types: quantitative, categorical, and text.
In genomics, textual annotations (e.g., 'BRCA2' gene) are important and are distinguished from categorical data, being visualized as textual representations.
More information on parallels between features in genomics data and other domain data (e.g., geospatial data) can be found in a survey paper [38].
Genomics researchers perform analytical tasks with data visualizations to explore genomic features and answer critical domain questions.
A review of genomics visualization tasks can be found in the survey by Nusrat et al. [38].
Through a thematic analysis of the tasks in the survey using the multi-level task typology of Brehmer & Munzner [6], genomics analysis tasks were categorized into three low-level query tasks.
The 'Identify' task involves analyzing features in a genomic region of interest to read a specific feature value.
For the 'Identify' task, an example is navigating to a gene A and checking its expression level.
The 'Compare' task involves comparing features located in multiple genomic regions.
For the 'Compare' task, an example is comparing the gene expression level between gene A and gene B.

The 'Overview' task involves looking at a larger genomic region or a whole genome to get an overview of the attributes of a feature set and identify interesting patterns such as outliers, clusters, or trends.
For the 'Overview' task, an example is identifying regions with many mutations.
The tasks and data introduced in this section play a critical role in the design of the GenoREC system.

Ada is a genomics researcher working at a cancer research institute.
Ada wants to develop a visualization to analyze genetic data obtained from three different files: a BED file, a VCF file, and a BIGWIG file.
The BED1 file stores the location of genes linked with certain diseases.
The VCF1 file stores structural variant events of a cancer patient.

Ada wants to compare the quantitative values of the BIGWIG file between different regions.
Ada wants to understand if specific genetic features in BED1 and VCF1 tracks contribute to the measurement of the BIGWIG file.
Ada visualizes the data using conventional genomics visualization tools such as UCSC Genome Browser, IGV Browser, and WashU Epigenome Browser.
Conventional genomics visualization tools can create visuals for specific data types.
Ada is unable to use a single tool to look at all her data and combine different file types for integrated analysis.
Ada spends a lot of time working across tools and makes compromises on her analyses.
Conventional tools are tightly coupled with default visualization techniques.
Ada would like to explore alternative visualization techniques and easily customize her visualizations.
Conventional tools do not consider Ada’s task, placing a burden on her to follow design guidelines to identify the best encoding.
Without task guidance, Ada may choose a misleading visualization.
Ada decides to try GenoREC to get a recommendation for a visualization that supports her requirements and steers her towards the final plots.

GenoREC was developed through an iterative design process.
Existing literature in recommendation systems and genomics visualization, including genomics visualization tasks, was analyzed to identify an initial set of system design goals.
A formative study was conducted with five domain experts to solicit feedback on the recommendation output, user interface, and system workflow.
Experts were interviewed to understand their genomics visualization authoring process and current challenges.
None of the experts involved in the studies are authors of this paper.

Input from experts and common design suggestions from prior work on general recommender systems and visualization recommendation systems were combined to identify goals for further development of GenoREC.

GenoREC is a novel visualization recommendation system for the analysis of genomics data.
The GenoREC system design and recommendation workflow are summarized in Fig. 1 (Bottom).
GenoREC consists of a front-end user interface that allows users to specify their input requirements to the system.
The front-end user interface of GenoREC allows users to browse the recommended visualizations.
The back-end recommendation model of GenoREC generates visualization recommendations.
The back-end recommendation model generates design configurations for appropriate visualizations given the user input.
The Input Compiler and Output Compiler modules orchestrate the exchange of information between the front-end and back-end.
A key design aspect of GenoREC is its modular architecture.
The modular architecture ensures that individual components are easy to update without affecting other system modules.
GenoREC’s user interface is implemented in JavaScript, HTML, and CSS.
The back-end recommendation model is published as a standalone JavaScript library on NPM.
GenoREC uses Gosling, a grammar-based visualization toolkit for genomics, for rendering recommendation.
GenoREC’s knowledge-based recommendation model recommends domain-specific visualizations based on visualization theory and best practices from the genomics domain.
The model is built on guidelines which map domain-specific input requirements to an appropriate output visualization.
The input and output space of GenoREC’s model is presented in this section.
The recommendation knowledge used by GenoREC is presented in this section.
The algorithm which allows the system to use the recommendation knowledge to generate the visualizations is described in this section.
The data input into GenoREC is divided into four categories: the assembly build, data type (quantitative, categorical, and text), feature set (feature extent and density), and connection.
The recommendation model expects the tasks (identify, compare, overview) as inputs.
The data and task input are discussed in Sect. 3.
GenoREC’s model breaks down the recommendation task into six intermediate steps: Encoding, Alignment, Layout, Partition, Arrangement, and Interactivity.
Each of these six components contains a set of possible output options as shown in Fig. 1B.
One of the main contributions of GenoREC is the use of sequential order to better reflect the dependencies between these components.
To determine the current order of components, we reviewed the genomics visualization taxonomy [38].
For each part of the taxonomy, we determined precursor steps.
We noticed that it was not possible to recommend an orthogonal 'Arrangement' if the 'Layout' of the tracks were circular.
This exercise allowed us to develop the sequence and led to the creation of the sequential model.
The sequential order of components ensures that the GenoREC system can accurately recommend visualizations.
We provide an overview of each component in the order GenoREC’s recommendation model determines them.
The encoding component identifies the visual mark and channel pair to encode attributes in a genomics dataset.
In genomics visualizations, there are four visual marks: point, line, rectangle ('rect'), and text.
There are also four channels: position, length, saturation, and hue.
The full list of combinations of marks and channels supported in GenoREC are visually depicted in Fig. 1B.
The alignment component identifies if the encodings from the Encoding component (C1) can be stacked or overlayed.
Stacked alignment applies encodings to individual tracks and then vertically stacks them.
A track refers to a unit visualization that corresponds to common visualization types.
Stacked alignment is used as the default option since it is the most frequent alignment in genomics visualizations.
Fig. 3A shows an example of stacked alignment where BED1 and VCF1 files are shown as two separate tracks that are vertically stacked.
The overlayed alignment merges encodings into a single track.
The Layout component selects the layout to display a track in the genomics visualization.
GenoREC supports three layouts: linear, circular, and space-filling.
The space-filling layout includes examples such as the Hilbert curve.
The partition component decides whether the chromosomes should be displayed in a contiguous track, where chromosomes are placed end-to-end.
The partition component decides whether the chromosomes should be displayed in a segregated manner, where each chromosome is independently displayed as a separate track.
Partition happens at a track level.
If a visualization has multiple tracks, GenoREC determines the division of each track.
The arrangement component is responsible for selecting the arrangement of multiple views.
In this paper, a view refers to a combination of one or multiple tracks.
Fig 3B represents two views, each consisting of two tracks from two data files.
The main difference between arrangement and partition is that arrangement is applied between views instead of between tracks.
In GenoREC, views with linear tracks can be arranged as parallel, adjacent, or orthogonal.
The orthogonal arrangement allows the creation of adjacency matrices for visualizing genomics data with a complete network connection between two sequences.
If views have a circular layout, GenoREC only permits parallel and adjacent arrangements.
The interactivity component is responsible for identifying proper interaction patterns for genomics visualization.
GenoREC supports two interaction patterns: coordinated interaction and focus+context.
In the coordinated interaction pattern, all tracks within a view have coordinated zooming and panning interactions.
The focus+context pattern allows users to focus on a specific portion of the genome while maintaining the context of the genome location.
This section presents the main design guidelines that shape the recommendation for GenoREC.
GenoREC uses best practices and domain-knowledge in combination (G2).
The selection of channels depends on the attribute types and low-level analytical tasks users want to perform with the visualization.
Experimental studies by Cleveland & McGill [9] and Heer & Bostock [15] ranked visual channels in terms of their accuracy to identify and compare quantitative data.
Based on the results of these studies, GenoREC maps quantitative values using position and length channels.
Fig. 5 shows the Decision Matrix for the Encoding component (C1).
Rows in the Decision Matrix represent the visual encodings.
Columns in the Decision Matrix represent the factors that affect the encoding selection.
A cell in the matrix with a value of 1 indicates that the encoding supports the factor.
An empty cell in the matrix represents a value of -1, indicating that the factor is not supported.
GenoREC allows mapping quantitative values of the color saturation channel for an overview task.
In overview tasks, users are looking for patterns, not individual values.
Color saturation can show variation in data for pattern search.
For categorical attributes, GenoREC uses categorical color schemes based on the ranking proposed by Mackinlay [30].
GenoREC supports overlayed alignments for genomics visualizations with multiple tracks only if the tracks are from the same file.
Overlaying tracks from different files can lead to occlusion due to the superposition of multiple marks at the same location.
GenoREC only supports overlaying position and color channels because they can co-exist without causing occlusion.
If a visualization has two tracks with position channels and one track with a color channel, GenoREC will combine the first position channel with the color channel.
This combination will lead to stacked and overlayed tracks.
In GenoREC, layouts are selected based on the input data and task descriptions, and the visual encoding set in the encoding component.
Waldner et al. [54] found that length and position channels make it easier to identify and compare visual representations in linear layouts.
This study recommends linear layouts when length and position are used in the encoding component for identifying and comparing tasks.
In overview tasks, where the user’s goal is to look for trends and patterns, GenoREC recommends both circular layouts and linear layouts.
GenoREC suggests parallel or orthogonal arrangements in linear layouts for inter-connectivity data.
Selection between parallel and orthogonal arrangements depends on the type of network data.
For dense networks, GenoREC recommends orthogonal arrangements.
For other cases, GenoREC recommends parallel arrangements.
For circular layouts, GenoREC recommends adjacent arrangements when there is a network connection.
Adjacent arrangements are one of the most common use cases with circular layouts in the domain.
Meyer et al. [33] used a circular adjacent layout for visualizing interconnection between different parts of a sequence.
The adjacent circular arrangement allows the analyst to look at overall connections between sequences in a space-efficient manner.
GenoREC gives preference to empirically backed design guidelines.
When there is a lack of empirical results, GenoREC factors the genomics-specific knowledge for the recommendation.
GenoREC recommends color saturation encoding used for commonly used heatmap visualizations for overview tasks.
There is no conclusive evidence that negates the use of color saturation encoding for overview tasks.
The knowledge for recommendation is represented and stored as a decision matrix in GenoREC’s model.
For each component (C1–C6) in Sect. 6.1.1, there is a distinct decision matrix.
The decision matrix for the Encoding component (C1) is shown in Fig. 5.
The rows in the matrix represent all the possible output options.
The columns in the matrix represent input factors that affect the output selection.
The cells in the matrix represent if the corresponding output (row) can support the corresponding input item (column).
GenoREC encodes the relationship between input and output as a binary value.
A cell with a dark circle represents a value of 1, meaning the output is supported by the corresponding input column.
In the 'Quant.' column (Fig. 5), all the cells corresponding to position (e.g., 'Point'), length (e.g., 'Rect'), and saturation (i.e., 'Saturation') have a value of 1.
Since the hue channel is not used to represent quantitative data, all cells corresponding to the hue channel have a value of 1 (i.e., empty cells).
Representing recommendation knowledge as binary-valued features allows GenoREC to use a similarity computation technique to rank the output of each component (C1–C6).
GenoREC uses the ranking for recommendation.
GenoREC computes the similarity between the input and all the output items in the product matrix using a cosine similarity metric.
The cosine similarity score expects two vectors of equal size and generates a score in the range of [-1,1].
GenoREC’s algorithm generates an input vector for each recommendation component based on the features given in the column headers of the decision matrix.
GenoREC scores the similarity of the input vector with all rows of the decision matrix.
A higher cosine similarity score closer to 1 means that the two vectors are more similar.
A lower cosine similarity score closer to -1 means the two vectors are dissimilar.
These scores are used for ranking in the GenoREC recommendation system.
GenoREC recommends the output item with the highest score.

In this example, all the visual encodings come from different sources and have different features.

The BED file is placed on the top and others are below it.
All the tracks in this component are aligned automatically based on reference genomes.
GenoREC determines the layout based on the encoding, alignment, and tasks.
The space-filling layout, such as the Hilbert curve, can only show a single track.
The circular layout is not conducive for comparing quantitative data in the BIGWIG file.

In this example, GenoREC recommends the 'Contiguous' partition to facilitate comparison.

GenoREC identifies arrangement based on the existence of network data, layout (C3), and tasks.
In the current example, GenoREC’s decision is based on the comparison task.
A single-view visualization can be difficult to compare two regions in the genomes, especially if they are distant, e.g., Chromosome 1 and Chromosome 18.

GenoREC’s user interface is divided into two panels: data and task descriptions.
GenoREC’s user interface includes a recommendation panel.
GenoREC’s UI allows users to specify domain-specific data formats such as BIGWIG, BED, BEDPE, SEG, VCF, and COOLER.
GenoREC’s UI allows users to specify tasks to the system.

Each data description card in GenoREC has six input fields: Assembly Build (coordinate system 1), Assembly Build (coordinate system 2), Quantitative, Categorical, Text, Feature Extent, Feature Density, and Connection.

Through GenoREC’s interface, analysts can try many different combinations of data input and see the recommendations without going through the data collection and processing pipeline.

The gallery-based interface supports easy comparison of the recommended options.
The recommended visualizations are updated when users add or modify the data or task specifications.

Users can export a Gosling JSON specification and directly load its online editor to customize the visualization further.
GenoREC was evaluated in a two-phase user study.
Qualitative feedback was gathered from domain experts to validate the recommendation output.
Qualitative feedback was gathered from domain experts to validate the user interface design.
A quantitative evaluation was conducted to measure the utility of GenoREC’s recommendation given a set of data and analysis task combinations.
The Harvard Institutional Review Board determined that these studies did not require research approval under federal regulations.
All participants were volunteers.
Participants were recruited through advertisements on various Slack teams in the computational biology and genomics communities and Twitter.
Study materials from both studies, including the stimuli, tasks, and data analysis code, are included in the Supplemental Material and on OSF (https://osf.io/y73pt/).
This study sought to answer the question: 'Does the output from the recommendation system match experts' expectations?'
Answering this question is important because it validates the recommendation rules applied by GenoREC.
The validation of the recommendation rules ensures that GenoREC's subsequent implementation is valid.
Feedback from this study helped refine GenoREC’s design goals.
Feedback from this study helped improve the user interface and the system’s overall workflow.
Five domain experts were recruited for the formative study.
The participants had experience at the intersection of genomics and visualization ranging from 8–20 years.
The study was designed as a semi-structured interview lasting an hour.
Participants were presented with three different data analysis scenarios in the form of short paragraphs of text.
One example scenario was: 'Given a set of BED files with human and mouse genome, identify regions where the data is highly conserved.'
Participants were asked to describe an appropriate visualization for each scenario.
Participants were asked to use GenoREC and comment on the accuracy of the recommended visualization.
At the end of the interview, participants were encouraged to provide feedback on the user interface.
All responses were analyzed by open coding and thematic analysis.
Most participants found GenoREC’s recommendations accurate and only required minor modifications for the scenarios included in the study.
This feedback led to the export feature in GenoREC’s user interface.

One participant expected the visualizations to include additional biological contexts such as gene annotation track and ideogram plots that provide a summary of chromosomes coupled with genomic location information.
An option to add a gene annotation track and ideograms to the visualization in GenoREC was added.
Another participant asked for an additional interactive component as a tabular view in the GenoREC interface that enables a faster lookup of gene location.
Since we mainly focused on the recommendation of visual representations in the GenoREC interface, the tabular view is not included.
We plan to add the tabular view feature to further enable effective visual exploration of genomics data.
GenoREC’s user interface was well-received, and participants understood the data and task descriptions.
One participant stated that it is possible to further abstract the domain-specific file inputs.
We decided to keep data descriptions in domain-specific terminology because other participants found it helpful.
In the second part of the study, we conducted a controlled within-subject quantitative study.
The study measured the difference in utility between GenoREC’s top-ranked visualizations and mid-ranked visualizations for a given set of datasets and analysis tasks.
The qualitative study provided feedback on the accuracy of the recommendation.
The study aimed to evaluate if the recommendation would be useful for a broader group of people working in genomics.

There were a total of nine data and task scenarios (Scenario 1–9) in the study.
The scenarios are designed to provide a comprehensive coverage of three factors: features, attributes, and tasks.
In Scenario 1, the feature combinations are point and sparse with no connection, the attribute used is categorical, and it is an identify task.
The scenarios cover all feature types (point, segment, contiguous, sparse, and network) at least once.

Tasks were balanced among identify, compare, and overview.
GenoREC was used to generate and score all possible visualizations that can be rendered by Gosling for the data and tasks of a given scenario.
The visualization with the top score was selected as the 'GenoREC stimulus'.
The visualization with the score closest to the median of the score distribution was selected as the 'alternate stimulus'.
If GenoREC recommends multiple top and median ranked visualizations with the same score, one of them is randomly selected as a stimulus.

Using subjective responses from domain users presents a practical way of assessing visualization recommendations for genomics.
We present a sequential recommendation model for genomics visualization.
To develop the sequential model, visualization techniques in genomics were broken down into multiple components (e.g., encoding, layout) and order was added to them.
The sequential method can be applied in other domains and visualization techniques.

Tree visualizations can be decomposed into three components based on a visualization taxonomy: 'Representation' (explicit, implicit, hybrid), 'Alignment' (parallel, radial, free), and 'Dimensionality' (2D, 3D, hybrid).
Tree visualization experts can determine the dependencies between components, such as whether 'Representation' of tree visualizations should be determined before 'Dimensionality'.
After ordering the components, domain experts can systematically curate recommendation knowledge for each component and create a sequential recommendation model for tree visualizations.
The sequential model may not apply universally across all domains and visualization techniques.

Applying the sequential model to infographics can be challenging because they offer a lot of design freedom, making it difficult to identify their design space and decompose visualization into smaller components.

Using a sequential model can simplify the process of designing a knowledge-based recommendation model for domains and visualization techniques where it is possible to break down visualization into components and apply order to them.
We anticipate the sequential model to be adopted more in the future.
GenoREC’s recommendation model can be updated by changing each component’s output items and decision factors.
Introducing a new glyph encoding in the Encoding component (C1) requires adding a new row to the decision matrix.
Adding additional decision factors requires adding a new column to the decision matrix of each component.
Factoring in user preferences for recommended encodings involves adding a new column in the decision matrix to store the relationship between encoding output and the user-preference factor.
Component-level changes in GenoREC are straightforward as they do not affect other aspects of the model.
Extending the recommendation model to handle a new component could be challenging.
Adding a new component requires careful analysis of its dependencies with all the other components, which can be complex if done post-hoc.
Researchers are recommended to err on the side of inclusion when identifying the components to be used with GenoREC’s recommendation approach.

Genomics data analysts rely heavily on visualization techniques for data interpretation.
GenoREC supports constructing appropriate interactive visualizations to make data interpretation more efficient.
Our design and algorithm can be extended to create other domain-specific visualization recommendations.
The visualization and task taxonomy must be well defined for creating domain-specific visualization recommendations.
Our work offers critical guidance for visualization researchers developing similar recommendation systems in other domains.

Gosling.js is a rendering toolkit for Gosling.

Gosling.js employs a TypeScript-based definition of the Gosling grammar.
Gosling.js consists of three main components: a compiler, a renderer, and a HiGlass client.
The compiler translates a Gosling specification into a HiGlass-interpretable view configuration.
The HiGlass client interprets the view configuration and fetches the data needed for rendering.
Using the data, the Gosling.js renderer displays individual tracks.

HiGlass preprocesses data to store aggregated information, such as nearby quantitative values or filtered values, for given genomic regions and resolutions.
The HiGlass client considers the regional information of Gosling.js visualizations, such as genomic regions and zoom levels, and fetches appropriate tiles from the source data.
The HiGlass client passes the fetched tiles to Gosling.js for visualization.

The Grammar of Graphics decomposes visualizations into abstracted components.
Data needs to be stored in an abstracted and consistent format, such as a tabular format, to facilitate the Grammar of Graphics approach.
Genomics data is stored in a wide range of text-based, binary, or compressed file formats, many of which are not tabular.
Grammars that expect tabular data require users to convert their data before visualizing it, which is inefficient and often not feasible.
The need for data conversion creates a conflict between domain specificity and data scalability.
Asking users to perform data transformation simplifies the rendering process of the grammar but places an enormous burden on users.
Data visualization software is typically employed in genomics data analysis alongside many other analysis tools in an iterative fashion.
Requiring users to convert gigabytes of data for each tool is unrealistic.

If the grammar supports domain-specific file formats and can transform data into tabular formats on the fly before encoding, domain specificity and data scalability can be addressed without burdening users.
On-the-fly data transformation is computationally expensive or impractical for large and complex genomics datasets, leading to data scalability issues.
This represents a significant barrier for developing domain-specific visualization grammars for domains dealing with large and complex data like genomics.
The HiGlass data visualization infrastructure allowed us to overcome the trade-off between domain specificity and data scalability.

Gosling is a grammar-based toolkit for scalable and interactive genomics data visualization.
Gosling balances expressiveness for multi-scale and multifocus visualizations.

The goal was to address the shortcomings of existing approaches for genomics visualization, particularly concerning customizability.
The capabilities of the grammar and the proposed toolkit were demonstrated through a series of examples.

Developing a domain-specific grammar and an accompanying toolkit can potentially overcome several critical limitations of general-purpose visualization grammars.
This work encourages the development of visualization grammars for other domains with unique domain-specific data types, visual representations, and analysis tasks.
Gosling will enable notable progress in genomics data visualization by providing a foundation for the design of novel scalable, interactive, multi-view visualizations.
Gosling removes common barriers such as limited expressiveness of template-based approaches and data scalability.
Gosling will enable broader participation in visualization design and implementation in genomics.

The recommended method uses a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) framework.
RAG is a widely adopted approach that combines a model’s parameters with external non-parametric memory to generate language.
RAG overcomes the limitations of language models in domain-specific tasks.
RAG consists of two stages: a retriever and a generator.
The retriever takes the user’s query and maps both the query and documents from an external corpus into a high-dimensional vector space using a shared embedding model.
The retriever identifies the most relevant documents by calculating similarities (e.g., Euclidean distance) between the query vector and document vectors.
The generator, often a pre-trained large language model (LLM), uses the content of retrieved documents to produce natural language text that satisfies both syntactic and semantic requirements.
The prompt input to the generator is optimized through prompt engineering to guide the model in generating the most relevant output.
The recommendation framework is divided into two stages based on RAG: the similar sample retriever and the configuration generator.
The Similar Sample Retriever was developed to search for samples related to bioinformatics analysts' queries.
